records.title: Blackheath to Greenwich: the slow way down the hill
records.summary: Start with village shops, cross the open heath and enter Greenwich Park from above. The famous view comes later; the quieter route towards it is the real pleasure.
keywords: Blackheath to Greenwich Walk: A Scenic London Route
records.content: Most Greenwich visits begin at the river and climb towards the Observatory. Starting in Blackheath reverses the effort and improves the story. You arrive quickly from central London, spend time in a neighbourhood with its own rhythm, cross a wide patch of sky and then descend through Greenwich Park as the city gradually appears. The route is simple enough to improvise. Its strength lies in the optional turns: a second hand bookshop, a flower garden, an old oak, a less crowded viewpoint and one or two exceptional interiors at the end. Begin in Blackheath, not at the station exit Blackheath is around fifteen minutes by train from London Bridge, but do not hurry straight towards the park. The streets near the station reward a short circuit: independent shops, cafés and the kind of local bookshop where browsing can easily become the first delay of the day. Then cross the heath. The openness is the point. Canary Wharf and the City appear on the horizon, but the immediate landscape refuses the density usually associated with London. On windy days the exposure is real; bring an extra layer even when the centre feels mild. Ranger’s House stands near the edge of Greenwich Park and can become a separate visit when open. If not, use it as a landmark and enter the park nearby. Take the quieter side of Greenwich Park The direct route to the Observatory is obvious and often busy. A better first move is through the Flower Garden, where the paths feel more enclosed and the park reveals itself gradually. From there, look for Queen Elizabeth’s Oak. The ancient tree has long since fallen, but its remains and the stories attached to it make a surprisingly effective pause. One Tree Hill is the essential detour. Its viewpoint sits east of Observatory Hill and looks across the Thames from a quieter angle. The path is steep, but the view preserves more foreground and feels less like a queue for the same photograph. New seating makes it a good place to stop. If mobility or time is limited, remain on the main paths and head towards the familiar General Wolfe viewpoint instead. The route still works; it simply becomes more direct. Descend through layers of Greenwich From the hill, the geometry of the Queen’s House and Old Royal Naval College lines up towards the river. Walking down converts a famous panorama into a sequence of real spaces. The Queen’s House is worth entering when open, particularly for the Tulip Stairs, whose blue spiral is far more delicate than the building’s formal exterior suggests. Continue to the Old Royal Naval College. The grounds are free to cross and remain impressive even without a ticket. The Chapel of St Peter and St Paul is open daily during normal visitor hours; the Painted Hall requires paid admission, currently sold with year round return access. Its scale makes it a strong finale if you still have energy. Greenwich Market is nearby, but it is better treated as an optional reward than an obligatory ending. On crowded weekends, a riverside walk or a quieter café may be more pleasant. Distance and timing The basic walk is roughly 5 kilometres, depending on your route through the park. With the Flower Garden, One Tree Hill, interiors and Blackheath browsing, it can easily become 7 kilometres and occupy most of a day. Allow at least two hours without stops and three to five for the version that makes the journey worthwhile. The overall direction is downhill, but there are short climbs and some steep paths. After heavy rain, softer routes in the park may be muddy. Pedestrian gate times change seasonally, so check the Royal Parks page if you plan a very early or late walk. Why this direction is better Ending at Greenwich gives you more options: trains, DLR, buses or a boat back towards central London. More importantly, the route builds naturally. It begins with ordinary local life, opens onto landscape and finishes among some of London’s grandest architecture. Greenwich’s famous view is not the destination. It is the moment when the whole walk finally explains where you have been going. Take the slow way down. The landmarks will still be there, but they will arrive with context rather than all at once.

records.title: The City of London dragon walk: follow the boundary most people miss
records.summary: White dragons stand guard where the City begins. Link them together and a familiar business district turns into a walk through boundaries, lost gates and stubborn fragments of old London.
keywords: City of London Dragon Walk: Route and History
records.content: Most people enter the City of London without noticing the moment it happens. The traffic continues, the buildings barely pause and there is no wall to cross. Look up, however, and a white dragon may be clutching a red and white shield above the road. These boundary markers turn an administrative line into a physical walking route. Following them is less about collecting every statue than learning where the City ends, why certain streets matter and how much history hides in places designed for movement. Why dragons guard the City A pair of dragons has supported the City’s shield in its coat of arms since the early seventeenth century. The boundary markers seen today were installed at important entry points, many in the late twentieth century, each dragon holding the heraldic shield. They are often mistaken for griffins. The wings, claws and reptilian body make the City’s intended creature clear, even if heraldry is not your usual hobby. Once you recognise the silhouette, the markers become difficult to unsee. The grandest examples announce major approaches; smaller dragons perch on columns beside roads that have lost their ceremonial importance. Together they describe a border that remains legally meaningful even where it feels invisible at street level. A route, not a treasure hunt There is no single compulsory order. A satisfying western section begins near the Temple Bar dragon on Fleet Street, continues around the Temple and Victoria Embankment, then turns towards Blackfriars and the north western edge of the City. An eastern section can pick up markers around Aldgate, Bishopsgate and the approaches to London Bridge. Trying to join every dragon in one outing creates a long, stop start walk. Splitting the circuit into west and east gives more time for the places between them: Smithfield, St Bartholomew the Great, the Barbican, Spitalfields, riverside lanes and the remains of streets shaped by former gates. Use the dragons as punctuation rather than the entire story. A marker beside a six lane road may not be beautiful, but it tells you that this precise crossing once deserved a formal welcome. The details worth noticing Look at the direction each dragon faces and the form of its base. Some stand alone as monuments; others seem to have been squeezed into modern street furniture. The repeated shield creates continuity, while differences in scale reveal which entrances the City wanted to make ceremonial. The surroundings are equally important. At London Bridge, the boundary aligns with one of the City’s oldest approaches. Near Temple, legal London presses against financial London. Around Aldgate and Bishopsgate, the names of vanished gates survive even when the structures do not. This is also a good walk for spotting the City’s smaller obsessions: plaques fixed high on walls, parish boundaries, old ward names and pieces of architecture preserved at improbable angles beneath newer buildings. Planning the walk Wear comfortable shoes and expect diversions. Construction, security barriers and traffic crossings can make the most direct line unpleasant. A map is useful, but do not treat a missing dragon as failure: some markers are easy to pass when trees, buses or road signs block the view. Weekends reduce commuter pressure, although parts of the City become very quiet and cafés close earlier. Weekdays provide more life but demand patience at busy junctions. Early morning offers the cleanest photographs. For a shorter version, choose three or four markers and connect them with one strong destination: One Leadenhall terrace, the Barbican, St Bartholomew the Great or the riverside. The route works best when the dragons lead somewhere rather than becoming the only purpose. What the walk changes The City is often described vertically through towers and viewpoints. The dragons make you read it horizontally, along its edge. Streets that seem unrelated begin to form a perimeter, and names such as Aldgate or Bishopsgate recover their literal meaning. The dragons do not reveal a lost wall. They reveal how often we cross a boundary without asking who drew it. By the end, the creatures themselves may be less interesting than the habit they teach: look above traffic height, question official symbols and pay attention whenever London quietly announces that one place has become another.

records.title: One Leadenhall terrace: London’s best new low-level view?
records.summary: This is not another race to the top of the skyline. Four floors above Leadenhall Market, the terrace succeeds because the City remains close enough to read.
keywords: One Leadenhall Public Terrace: Free London View
records.content: London’s newest viewpoints usually sell altitude. The Terrace at One Leadenhall offers something more useful: proximity. From Level 4, Leadenhall Market is directly below, church towers sit among office blocks and the modern City feels less like a postcard than a complicated piece of urban machinery. It is free, requires no ticket under normal arrangements and takes only a few minutes to reach from street level. That makes it easy to add to a City walk without arranging the day around it. Why a low terrace works At first, four floors may not sound much in a district of towers. Yet that is precisely the advantage. High viewing platforms flatten London into a distant panorama; here, the relationships between buildings remain visible. You can see the roof of Leadenhall Market, the stone and brick fragments that survived around it, and the much larger forms that now crowd the same streets. The planting and seating soften the space without turning it into a destination restaurant. It feels like a public terrace rather than a bar with an inconvenient obligation to buy something. Stay for ten minutes on a busy day or bring a coffee and give the view longer. Both approaches make sense. Finding the entrance The dedicated entrance is on Whittington Avenue at number 8. Two lifts run directly to the terrace lobby on Level 4. This matters because approaching from Leadenhall Street can make the access look more mysterious than it is; do not wander through unrelated office entrances. There is no standard advance booking and entry is free. Capacity is limited, however, and security or temporary closures can affect access. The terrace is outdoors, so strong wind or poor weather may also change the experience. Check the official page if you are making a special trip. What to look for Begin with Leadenhall Market. From above, its Victorian roof reads as a complete structure rather than a decorative ceiling glimpsed between shops. Then look beyond it: the Walkie Talkie, older church towers and a compressed collection of roofs show how little empty space the City contains. Look for St Paul’s Cathedral playing hide and seek between the buildings. The view changes rapidly with the light. Midday reveals detail; late afternoon brings reflections and sharper contrasts between stone and glass. After dark, the terrace becomes more atmospheric, although the historic fabric below is harder to read. Photographers should bring a moderate wide angle lens rather than expecting an unobstructed 360 degree panorama. Railings, planting and the surrounding tower all shape the composition. They are not defects; they explain where you are. Make it part of a better City walk A standalone visit can be brief, so pair it with places that benefit from the same close looking. Walk through Leadenhall Market, inspect the medieval street pattern around St Michael Cornhill, or continue to the Monument and the riverside. The boundary dragons offer another ready made thread through the district. The terrace also works as a pause between Liverpool Street and London Bridge. Instead of treating the City as a zone to cross quickly, use the elevated view to choose what deserves attention at ground level. Is it worth going out of your way? Yes, if you are already in central London or enjoy architecture. No, if what you want is the highest possible view or a grand indoor observatory. One Leadenhall is modest by skyscraper standards and better for it. The pleasure is not seeing more of London. It is seeing a small, dense part of it more clearly. Free viewpoints often become popular because they mimic paid attractions. This one is more distinctive: it gives the City back its scale, layers and awkward collisions. Four floors are enough.

records.title: Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration: beyond the familiar drawings
records.summary: London’s new home for illustration uses a beautifully restored industrial site to make the case that drawings are not the supporting act. They are the story.
keywords: Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration Guide
records.content: The name above the door may be Quentin Blake’s, but the Centre is not a monument to one illustrator. Its real subject is the restless territory between an idea and an image: picture books, comics, reportage, murals, theatre work and the drawings that never become finished publications. That breadth is what makes the visit worthwhile. You may arrive expecting the loose ink lines most closely associated with Roald Dahl and leave thinking about illustration as performance, argument or private experiment. A new use for New River Head The Centre opened in June 2026 at New River Head in Clerkenwell. The former waterworks buildings give the visit an atmosphere that a neutral white gallery would struggle to create. Brick, courtyards and traces of industry frame the exhibitions without overpowering them. It is compact enough to understand in one visit but not so small that the ticket feels like an entrance fee for a single room. Alongside the galleries there is a library, a creative studio, a café and a shop. The result feels closer to a working centre than a polished shrine. Start with Quentin Blake, then keep going The long running opening exhibition, Quentin Blake: Performance , brings together more than a hundred original works and looks at the influence of theatre on Blake’s practice. The useful surprise is how quickly the familiar style becomes unfamiliar again. Rough lines that seem spontaneous are shown as the product of timing, movement and repeated decisions. Do not reduce Blake to his collaborations with Dahl. His hospital commissions, independent books, adult work and experiments with scale show a much wider practice. Seen together, the drawings have the energy of people entering a stage rather than characters waiting obediently on a page. The other galleries widen the lens. Their exhibitions change, which is exactly why the Centre should not be treated as a one off destination. Check what is current before travelling, especially if a temporary show is the main reason for your visit. Look closely, not quickly Illustration often appears effortless because the final image has already solved its problems. Here, original drawings make hesitation visible: pencil marks beneath ink, changes in posture, empty space doing more work than expected. A framed sheet can reward several minutes, particularly when it sits beside another version of the same idea. The temptation is to photograph every witty image and move on. Resist it. Choose a handful of drawings and look at how the line controls pace, where the eye enters the page and what has deliberately been left out. The Centre is at its best when it teaches you to read an image with the patience usually reserved for text. How much time to allow Allow around 90 minutes for the exhibitions and longer if you plan to use the library, stop at the café or visit with children. The scale makes it easy to combine with the London Canal Museum, Exmouth Market or a walk through Clerkenwell, but cramming it between two larger museums would miss the point. The building is open Wednesday to Sunday. Exhibition admission is paid, with concessions, while some events and activities are free. Current exhibitions, prices and last entry times can change, so use the official visit page rather than an old listing. Who should go This is an obvious destination for illustrators, designers and families, but that description is too narrow. Anyone interested in how ideas become visible will find something here: the false confidence of a finished line, the comedy of a tiny gesture, or the politics carried by an image before a caption says anything. The Centre’s best trick is to make a drawing look less simple the longer you spend with it. Go for Quentin Blake if that is the hook you need. Stay for the evidence that illustration is not decoration around a story; very often, it is the part that tells us how to read it.

records.title: Trinity Buoy Wharf: London’s lighthouse at the edge of the Thames
records.summary: A lighthouse that never guided ships to sea, a composition designed to last a thousand years and one of east London’s strangest riverside corners.
keywords: Trinity Buoy Wharf: Lighthouse and Longplayer Guide
records.content: Trinity Buoy Wharf feels less like a conventional attraction than a pocket of London that avoided being tidied up. Shipping containers have become studios, experimental structures sit beside Victorian engineering and the Thames meets the Lea under the shadow of the O2. At the centre is London’s only lighthouse. It is not a polished heritage complex. People work here, events take over parts of the site and some doors will be closed when you visit. That incompleteness is part of the appeal. A lighthouse built for experiments The current Experimental Lighthouse was built in 1864 for Trinity House. Rather than warning ships from a dangerous coast, it was used to test lamps and equipment and to train lighthouse keepers. Michael Faraday, scientific adviser to Trinity House, carried out work on the site; a small structure nearby now houses The Faraday Effect , an installation by Ana Ospina. The lighthouse is normally open to visitors at weekends, with seasonal hours and free entry. The stairs are narrow and access is limited, so check the official listing before making a dedicated journey. Reaching the lantern level is worth it for the unusual view: the river, the Lea, Docklands and the O2 line up from a place that still feels slightly outside central London’s script. Listen to a thousand year composition Inside the lighthouse, Longplayer changes the scale of the visit. Conceived by Jem Finer, the composition began at midnight on 31 December 1999 and is designed to play without repetition for a thousand years. Its live listening post uses Tibetan singing bowls and a circular arrangement that makes the room feel part instrument, part observatory. The idea could have been a gimmick. In the lighthouse it becomes more persuasive. Industrial history, tidal water and a piece of music intended to outlast everyone listening to it make time feel unusually physical. Give it several quiet minutes rather than treating it as background sound. What else is on the wharf The site rewards a slow circuit. Look for the red lightship, container studios, public sculpture and the Faraday installation. Fatboy’s Diner adds a piece of American roadside fantasy, while the river’s edge provides one of the least familiar views towards the O2. Not every artwork or business keeps the same hours as the wharf. Think of the outdoor site as the reliable part and anything indoors as a bonus unless you have checked in advance. The wharf itself is open daily, except Christmas Day. Getting there East India on the DLR is the simplest station, followed by a walk through a landscape of roads, new housing and surviving industry. The route can feel counter intuitive near the Lea crossing, so save the final map section before leaving the station. Canning Town is another option but generally makes the approach longer. Arriving on foot is appropriate: the transition from ordinary streets to the buoy wharf is part of the experience. The site is also a strong addition to a wider walk around Leamouth, the Lower Lea and the Royal Docks. How long to allow Allow at least an hour for the outdoor site and closer to two if the lighthouse is open, you sit with Longplayer or stop for food. A bright day gives the clearest views; grey weather arguably suits the industrial textures better. Wind is the more important variable. Trinity Buoy Wharf is not hidden, exactly. It is simply placed where most London itineraries stop looking. Come for the novelty of a lighthouse in London. Stay for a site where engineering, art and the river still occupy the same untidy ground.

records.title: V&A East Storehouse: the museum that shows its workings
records.summary: Half a million objects, open storage and a museum that turns its backstage machinery into part of the visit. The scale is striking; the freedom to follow your own curiosity is the real point.
keywords: V&A East Storehouse: What to See and Know
records.content: V&A East Storehouse does not behave like a conventional museum. There is no prescribed march through period rooms and no attempt to make the collection look finished. Instead, the building exposes the storage systems, conservation work and unlikely neighbours that normally sit behind a museum’s public face. That distinction matters. The first impression is architectural — a cavernous hall, industrial shelving and objects visible across several levels — but the more interesting change is editorial. You are not being led through one tidy argument. You are being invited to notice connections for yourself. A collection store you can actually enter The Storehouse opened in 2025 at Here East, on the western edge of Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. It holds more than 500,000 objects, around 1,000 archives and hundreds of thousands of books. Those figures explain the scale, but not the experience. The Weston Collections Hall forms the centre of the public route. Displays are set into and around the working store, mixing familiar names with objects that would struggle to justify a permanent gallery of their own. A historic interior may sit near fashion, furniture, theatre material or a fragment of architecture. The lack of a neat hierarchy is productive: the collection feels less like a textbook and more like accumulated evidence of how people make things. This is not simply a warehouse with labels attached. Bridges, openings and long sightlines make the working collection legible without pretending that every object is permanently on display. Some areas remain operational; others offer close views of large pieces that could not easily appear at South Kensington. What is worth slowing down for The mistake is to treat the building as a checklist. Its value comes from wandering, looking up and allowing one object to redirect the visit. The small displays around the central hall are useful starting points, but the most memorable moments may be the accidental combinations between them. Notice the changes in scale. The building can move abruptly from something monumental to a small working detail: a label, a packing support, a conservation clue or an object placed temporarily in view. These transitions reveal that museums are not neutral containers. Decisions about storage, access, interpretation and care determine what the public gets to see. The Study Centre extends that idea. Through the V&A’s Order an Object service, material not currently on display can be requested for an appointment. The David Bowie Centre is also based here, giving the archive a permanent home while showing changing selections from it. Both reward more planning than a casual visit, so check the current arrangements before travelling. How long to allow A first visit can work in 90 minutes, but two to three hours is more realistic if you want to follow several threads without rushing. The open layout makes it easy to underestimate time: a display that looks small from the other side of the hall may contain enough detail to hold you for twenty minutes. There is no obligation to be comprehensive. Choose a level, follow a material or subject that catches your attention and leave something for another day. Free admission makes repeat visits a better strategy than trying to absorb half a million objects in one afternoon. Getting there without making it a transport exercise Hackney Wick is the most natural station. The walk through Here East is straightforward once you are on the correct side of the canal, although building names and large developments can make a short route feel less obvious than it is. Check the final walking section rather than relying only on the postcode. Stratford offers more rail and Underground connections, followed by a longer walk, a local bus or the Here East shuttle when it is running. In decent weather, arriving through the Olympic Park can become part of the visit rather than dead time. Who will get the most from it The Storehouse works particularly well for people interested in design, architecture, archives or the practical life of museums. It is also useful for repeat London visitors who know the main South Kensington galleries and want a different relationship with the same collection. It may be less satisfying if you want a short list of masterpieces and a clear route between them. The freedom is genuine, but it asks you to do some of the selecting. That is not a flaw; it is the proposition. Come for the visible scale. Stay for the smaller realisation that every museum display is the end of a much longer chain of choices. V&A East Storehouse is unusual not because its objects have never been seen, but because it changes what counts as the museum. Storage, research, cataloguing and conservation are no longer hidden support functions. They become part of the public experience — incomplete, occasionally overwhelming and far more interesting for it.
